claim: Systemic oxygen restriction (SOR) is prevalent in numerous clinical conditions, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
source: Systemic oxygen restriction (SOR) is prevalent in numerous clinical conditions, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and is associated with increased susceptibility to viral infections.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevalence of SOR in clinical conditions, drawing from established medical knowledge.

claim: Systemic oxygen restriction is associated with increased susceptibility to viral infections.
source: Systemic oxygen restriction (SOR) is prevalent in numerous clinical conditions, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and is associated with increased susceptibility to viral infections.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Low oxygen level diminishes CD8+ T cell anti-viral response in vivo.
source: We find that low oxygen level diminishes CD8+ T cell anti-viral response in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Respiratory restriction inhibits ATP-dependent matrix processes that are critical for mitochondrial-biogenesis.
source: We reveal that respiratory restriction inhibits ATP-dependent matrix processes that are critical for mitochondrial-biogenesis.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The respiratory restriction-mediated effect could be rescued by TCA cycle re-stimulation.
source: This respiratory restriction-mediated effect could be rescued by TCA cycle re-stimulation, which yielded increased mitochondrial matrix-localized ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing FCCP rescue in Figure 5.

claim: TCA cycle re-stimulation yields increased mitochondrial matrix-localized ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation.
source: This respiratory restriction-mediated effect could be rescued by TCA cycle re-stimulation, which yielded increased mitochondrial matrix-localized ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data in Figure 5E-G.

claim: The hypoxia-arrested CD8+ T cell anti-viral response could be rescued in vivo through brief exposure to atmospheric oxygen pressure.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that the hypoxia-arrested CD8+ T cell anti-viral response could be rescued in vivo through brief exposure to atmospheric oxygen pressure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Hypoxemia, reduced blood oxygen saturation, and tissue hypoxia are associated with multiple respiratory and circulatory diseases, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and congenital heart disease.
source: This is important field of research, since hypoxemia, reduced blood oxygen saturation, and tissue hypoxia are associated with multiple respiratory and circulatory diseases, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and congenital heart disease (Kent et al., 2011; Kaskinen et al., 2016; O'Brien and Smith, 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Patients with hypoxemia exhibit a higher prevalence of viral infections compared to healthy individuals.
source: Reportedly, such patients also exhibit a higher prevalence of viral infections compared to healthy individuals (Chaw et al., 2020; Kherad et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hypoxic conditions contribute to the formation of long-lasting effector cells.
source: Some have found that hypoxic conditions contribute to the formation of long-lasting effector cells (Phan and Goldrath, 2015; Phan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Respiratory restriction, mediated by inhibition of mitochondrial ATP synthase, arrests T cell activation.
source: Other studies have demonstrated that respiratory restriction, mediated by inhibition of mitochondrial ATP synthase, arrests T cell activation (Chang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Activated T cells undergo an early shift in cell metabolism, switching to aerobic glycolysis to support their expansion and cytotoxic function.
source: This is particularly interesting because activated T cells undergo an early shift in cell metabolism, in parallel to activation stimuli, switching to aerobic glycolysis to support their expansion and cytotoxic function (Gubser et al., 2013; van der Windt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mice challenged under chronic hypoxia exhibited a 10-fold decrease in Ki67-positive OVA-associated CD8+ T cells compared to mice challenged under atmospheric oxygen levels.
source: Mice challenged under chronic hypoxia exhibited a 10-fold decrease in Ki67-positive OVA-associated CD8+ T cells compared to mice challenged under atmospheric oxygen levels (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: The induction of systemic chronic hypoxia in vivo disrupts the CD8+ T cell response to viral infection.
source: These findings suggest that the induction of systemic chronic hypoxia in vivo disrupts the CD8+ T cell response to viral infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Naïve CD8+ T cells activated under hypoxic conditions exhibited reduced levels of the in vitro activation marker CD25 compared to cells activated under atmospheric oxygen levels.
source: In accordance with our in vivo findings and previous reports (Chang et al., 2013), naïve CD8+ T cells (Tn) activated under hypoxic conditions exhibited reduced levels of the in vitro activation marker CD25 (Figure 1I–J) and diminished proliferative capacity (Figure 1K–L) compared to cells activated under atmospheric oxygen levels.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1I-J.

claim: Naïve CD8+ T cells activated under hypoxic conditions exhibited diminished proliferative capacity compared to cells activated under atmospheric oxygen levels.
source: In accordance with our in vivo findings and previous reports (Chang et al., 2013), naïve CD8+ T cells (Tn) activated under hypoxic conditions exhibited reduced levels of the in vitro activation marker CD25 (Figure 1I–J) and diminished proliferative capacity (Figure 1K–L) compared to cells activated under atmospheric oxygen levels.
evidence: This is supported by proliferation data in Figure 1K-L.

claim: Human CD8+ T cells activated under hypoxic conditions exhibited a marked decrease in surface expression of CD25 and proliferative capacity.
source: As expected, and similar to the findings in mouse cells, human CD8+ T cells activated under hypoxic conditions exhibited a marked decrease in surface expression of CD25, and proliferative capacity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-G.

claim: CD8+ T cell activation is compromised during systemic chronic hypoxia.
source: Together, our findings demonstrate that CD8+ T cell activation is compromised during systemic chronic hypoxia.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Hypoxia does not significantly impact the proliferation or function of effector T cells.
source: It was previously demonstrated that although hypoxia negatively impacts naïve T cell proliferation after activation, it does not significantly impact the proliferation or function of effector T cells.
evidence: This is based on previous literature cited in the discussion.

claim: Hypoxia can improve effector T cell functions in vivo.
source: Moreover, some reports show that hypoxia can actually improve effector T cell functions in vivo (Doedens et al., 2013; Gropper et al., 2017; Makino et al., 2003; Vuillefroy de Silly et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: T cells acquire hypoxia tolerance during their activation.
source: These findings suggest that T cells acquire hypoxia tolerance during their activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous literature and the experimental design.

claim: CD8+ T cells exposed to hypoxia at the early time-point following activation exhibited impaired elevation of CD25 expression and decreased proliferative capacity.
source: Notably, CD8+ T cells exposed to hypoxia at the early time-point following activation exhibited impaired elevation of CD25 expression and decreased proliferative capacity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2B-E.

claim: Impairments in CD25 expression and proliferative capacity were partially prevented in cells transferred to hypoxic conditions at the late time-point following activation.
source: These impairments were partially prevented in cells transferred to hypoxic conditions at the late time-point following activation (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2B-E.

claim: Oligomycin partially mimics the effect induced by hypoxia, imposing cellular respiratory restriction.
source: To investigate the hypoxia-mediated inhibitory effect, we used the ATP synthase-specific inhibitor oligomycin, which partially mimics the effect induced by hypoxia , imposing cellular respiratory restriction (Chang et al., 2013; Solaini et al., 2010; Sgarbi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Oligomycin enables differentiation between indirect effects mediated by inhibition of the electron transport chain and the TCA cycle versus the direct effects caused by reduced mitochondrial ATP.
source: Importantly, it enables differentiation between indirect effects mediated by inhibition of the electron transport chain and the TCA cycle (Martínez-Reyes et al., 2016) versus the direct effects caused by reduced mitochondrial ATP (Lee and O'Brien, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activated CD8+ T cells treated with oligomycin at time-points earlier than 9 hr post-stimuli showed decreased CD25 expression and proliferation.
source: Activated CD8+ T cells treated with oligomycin at time-points earlier than 9 hr post-stimuli (T-Early) showed decreased CD25 expression and proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2G-J.

claim: When oligomycin was added at time-points later than 12 hr post-stimuli, a significant increase of CD25 expression and proliferation was observed.
source: However, when oligomycin was added at time-points later than 12 hr post-stimuli (T-Late), we observed a significant increase of CD25 expression and proliferation (Figure 2G–J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2G-J.

claim: There is a gradual metabolic rewiring process that promotes the development of a metabolic bypass of respiratory restriction in T-Late.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest a gradual metabolic rewiring process that promotes the development of a metabolic bypass of respiratory restriction in T-Late.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Both basal ECAR and maximal ECAR were comparable between T-Early and T-Late, and these rates were elevated with respect to Tn.
source: Interestingly, both basal ECAR (without oligomycin treatment) and maximal ECAR (with oligomycin treatment) were comparable between T-Early and T-Late, and these rates were elevated with respect to Tn (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by seahorse data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: The glucose-uptake rate did not substantially differ between Tn and the CD8+ T cells activated for 6, 9, or 12 hr.
source: The glucose-uptake rate did not substantially differ between Tn and the CD8+ T cells activated for 6, 9, or 12 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by 2-NBDG uptake data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: At 24 hr post-stimuli, a considerable increase in the amount of glucose uptake was observed.
source: At a later stage of the activation, 24 hr post-stimuli, we observed a considerable increase in the amount of glucose uptake.
evidence: This is supported by 2-NBDG uptake data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: T-Early exhibited higher levels of intracellular glucose 6-phosphate (G6P), and reduced glucose levels.
source: Specifically, T-Early exhibited higher levels of intracellular glucose 6-phosphate (G6P), and reduced glucose levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The secreted lactate concentration was substantially elevated in T-Early compared to Tn.
source: Similarly, the secreted lactate concentration was substantially elevated in T-Early compared to Tn (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Glycolysis-related metabolites did not significantly differ between T-Late and T-Early cells.
source: In contrast, glycolysis-related metabolites did not significantly differ between T-Late and T-Early cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E–F).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E-F.

claim: The development of tolerance to respiratory restriction is not correlated with increased glycolytic activity.
source: Collectively, our observations demonstrate that stimulated CD8+ T cells exhibited a marked increase of glycolytic metabolism at least 9 hr before they acquired tolerance to respiratory restriction. These findings indicate that the development of tolerance to respiratory restriction is not correlated with increased glycolytic activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolic data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mitochondria undergo robust biogenesis and extensive metabolic rewiring at ~12 hr after T cell activation.
source: Previous reports show that mitochondria undergo robust biogenesis and extensive metabolic rewiring at ~12 hr after T cell activation (Rambold and Pearce, 2018; Ron-Harel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stimulated CD8+ T cells derived from mitochondria-labeled mtDendra2 mice showed a substantial increase of mitochondrial mass at 12 hr post-stimuli.
source: Stimulated CD8+ T cells derived from mitochondria-labeled mtDendra2 mice (Pham et al., 2012) showed a substantial increase of mitochondrial mass at 12 hr post-stimuli, correlating with CD8+ T cell acquisition of tolerance to respiratory restriction (Figure 2K–L).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2K-L.

claim: T-Late cells exhibited a significant increase in spare respiratory capacity in comparison to T-Early.
source: Likewise T-Late cells exhibited a significant increase in spare respiratory capacity in comparison to T-Early (Figure 2M–N).
evidence: This is supported by seahorse data in Figure 2M-N.

claim: Upon CD8+ T cell activation, the development of tolerance to respiratory restriction is correlated with a gain of mitochondrial biomass linked to mitochondrial rewiring.
source: Thus, upon CD8+ T cell activation, the development of tolerance to respiratory restriction is correlated with a gain of mitochondrial biomass linked to mitochondrial rewiring (Ron-Harel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data in Figure 2 and citations.

claim: Oligomycin treatment yielded a marked increase of mono/di-phospho-nucleotides at the expense of tri-phospho-nucleotides in T-Early cells.
source: As expected, oligomycin treatment yielded a marked increase of mono/di-phospho-nucleotides at the expense of tri-phospho-nucleotides in T-Early cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data in Figure 3A.

claim: A similar effect of oligomycin on phospho-nucleotides was observed in hypoxia-resilient T-Late cells.
source: A similar effect was observed in hypoxia-resilient T-Late cells exposed to oligomycin (Figure 3B), suggesting that activated CD8+ T cells may function under increased AMP levels.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data in Figure 3B.

claim: Activated CD8+ T cells may function under increased AMP levels.
source: A similar effect was observed in hypoxia-resilient T-Late cells exposed to oligomycin (Figure 3B), suggesting that activated CD8+ T cells may function under increased AMP levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolomics data in Figure 3B.

claim: Treatment with oligomycin markedly increased the p-AMPK levels in treated naïve T cells.
source: Treatment with oligomycin, which is the typical positive control for AMPK activation, markedly increased the p-AMPK levels in treated naïve T cells.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 3C.

claim: Following activation, oligomycin only marginally increased the level of p-AMPK in respect to untreated activated control.
source: Interestingly following activation oligomycin only marginally increased the level of p-AMPK in respect to untreated activated control.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 3C.

claim: The response to oligomycin was comparable between T-Early and T-Late cells.
source: Importantly, the response to oligomycin was comparable between T-Early and T-Late cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 3C.

claim: The respiratory dependence during early T cell activation is not caused by an altered cellular response to reduced AMP levels in the cytoplasm.
source: Further, the respiratory dependence during early T cell activation is not caused by an altered cellular response to reduced AMP levels in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is an inference based on the p-AMPK data in Figure 3C.

claim: ANT2 is the dominant ADP/ATP translocator in murine CD8+ T cells, constituting approximately 90% of the total ANT protein.
source: ANT2 is the dominant ADP/ATP translocator in murine CD8+ T cells, constituting approximately 90% of the total ANT protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ANT2ko CD8+ T cells displayed substantially increased mitochondrial membrane polarization.
source: Importantly, ANT2ko CD8+ T cells displayed substantially increased mitochondrial membrane polarization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), indicating a decreased matrix ADP concentration.
evidence: This is supported by TMRM staining data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ANT2-deficient T cells exhibited intact activation-induced CD25 expression.
source: Surprisingly, ANT2-deficient T cells exhibited intact activation-induced CD25 expression (Figure 3D–E) and robust proliferative capacity (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3D-E.

claim: ANT2-deficient T cells exhibited robust proliferative capacity.
source: Surprisingly, ANT2-deficient T cells exhibited intact activation-induced CD25 expression (Figure 3D–E) and robust proliferative capacity (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3F-G.

claim: The ANT2ko-derived CD8+ T cells were still sensitive to respiratory restriction during early activation.
source: Notably, the ANT2ko-derived CD8+ T cells were still sensitive to respiratory restriction during early activation (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3D-G.

claim: CD8+ T cells stimulated in the presence of bongkrekic acid exhibited an increase of CD25 surface expression similar to the untreated control group.
source: CD8+ T cells stimulated in the presence of bongkrekic acid, at concentrations that increase mitochondrial membrane polarization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), exhibited an increase of CD25 surface expression (Figure 3H–I) and proliferation patterns (Figure 3J–K) that were similar to the untreated control group.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3H-I.

claim: CD8+ T cells stimulated in the presence of bongkrekic acid exhibited proliferation patterns similar to the untreated control group.
source: CD8+ T cells stimulated in the presence of bongkrekic acid, at concentrations that increase mitochondrial membrane polarization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), exhibited an increase of CD25 surface expression (Figure 3H–I) and proliferation patterns (Figure 3J–K) that were similar to the untreated control group.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3J-K.

claim: ATP generated by mitochondrial respiration is not required for cytoplasmic function of activated CD8+ T cell.
source: These key observations illustrate that ATP generated by mitochondrial respiration is not required for cytoplasmic function of activated CD8+ T cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ANT2ko and bongkrekic acid data in Figure 3.

claim: An upstream respiratory-restriction-coupled effect is a limiting factor underlying CD8+ T cells' sensitivity to respiratory restriction during early activation.
source: Furthermore, our results suggest that an upstream respiratory-restriction-coupled effect is a limiting factor underlying CD8+ T cells' sensitivity to respiratory restriction during early activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Mitochondrial-biogenesis and rewiring are critical checkpoints in T cell activation.
source: Mitochondrial-biogenesis and rewiring are critical checkpoints in T cell activation (Ron-Harel et al., 2016; Rambold and Pearce, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mitochondrial-biogenesis and rewiring rely on the availability of matrix-bond ATP, which is generated by substrate-level phosphorylation.
source: These cellular processes rely on the availability of matrix-bond ATP, which is generated by substrate-level phosphorylation, the metabolism of succinyl-CoA to succinate in the TCA cycle (Schwimmer et al., 2005; Chinopoulos et al., 2010; Bochud-Allemann and Schneider, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: mtDendra2-derived T-Early cells transferred to a hypoxic chamber exhibited reduced CD25 expression.
source: As expected, mtDendra2-derived T-Early cells transferred to a hypoxic chamber exhibited reduced CD25 expression (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4A-B.

claim: T-Early cells from the hypoxia group showed significantly reduced mtDendra2 expression.
source: Importantly, T-Early cells from the hypoxia group showed significantly reduced mtDendra2 expression (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4C-D.

claim: Oligomycin treatment during early activation of CD8+ T cells abrogated activation.
source: Similarly, oligomycin treatment during early activation of CD8+ T cells abrogated activation (Figure 4E–F) and inhibited the increase of mitochondrial mass that was observed in control mtDendra2-derived CD8+ T cells (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Oligomycin treatment during early activation inhibited the increase of mitochondrial mass that was observed in control mtDendra2-derived CD8+ T cells.
source: Similarly, oligomycin treatment during early activation of CD8+ T cells abrogated activation (Figure 4E–F) and inhibited the increase of mitochondrial mass that was observed in control mtDendra2-derived CD8+ T cells (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4G-H.

claim: Substantially higher mtDendra2 expression was observed in proliferating T-Late cells compared to undivided T-Late cells.
source: Interestingly, we observed substantially higher mtDendra2 expression in proliferating T-Late cells compared to undivided T-Late cells (Figure 4I), suggesting that respiratory restriction inhibits activation by disrupting mitochondrial-biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4I.

claim: Respiratory restriction inhibits activation by disrupting mitochondrial-biogenesis.
source: Interestingly, we observed substantially higher mtDendra2 expression in proliferating T-Late cells compared to undivided T-Late cells (Figure 4I), suggesting that respiratory restriction inhibits activation by disrupting mitochondrial-biogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mtDendra2 data in Figure 4I.

claim: Oligomycin treatment yielded markedly increased unpmt-Rnr levels in T-Early cells but not in T-Late cells.
source: Oligomycin treatment yielded markedly increased unpmt-Rnr levels in T-Early cells but not in T-Late cells (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4K.

claim: The ratios between unpmt-Rnr and its cleaved products, Rnr1 or Rnr2, were further increased in oligomycin-treated T-Early cells compared to T-Late cells.
source: Accordingly, we found that the ratios between unpmt-Rnr and its cleaved products, Rnr1 or Rnr2, were further increased in oligomycin-treated T-Early cells compared to T-Late cells (Figure 4L and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4L and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In T-Early cells, acute oligomycin treatment significantly increased the amounts of ubiquitinated TFAM and CH60 chaperone compared to controls without oligomycin treatment.
source: As expected, in T-Early cells, acute oligomycin treatment significantly increased the amounts of at least two central matrix proteins when compared to controls without oligomycin treatment. Specifically, T-Early cells exhibited increased abundances of ubiquitinated mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and the CH60 chaperone, which plays a role in the folding and assembly of newly imported proteins in the mitochondria.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 4M.

claim: Oligomycin-treated T-Late cells showed no substantial increase in ubiquitinated matrix proteins compared to untreated controls.
source: In line with the partial tolerance to oligomycin observed during late activation, oligomycin-treated T-Late cells showed no substantial increase in ubiquitinated matrix proteins compared to untreated controls (Figure 4M-N and its source data).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 4M-N.

claim: In samples from oligomycin-treated T-Early cells, leader peptides of several mitochondrial proteins whose mitochondrial import depends on matrix ATP were detected.
source: Furthermore, in samples from oligomycin-treated T-Early cells, we detected leader peptides of several mitochondrial proteins whose mitochondrial import depends on matrix ATP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: No relevant leader peptides were detected in any of the untreated samples or in the oligomycin-treated T-Late samples.
source: In contrast, no relevant leader peptides were detected in any of the untreated samples or in the oligomycin-treated T-Late samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: There is a matrix-specific energetic crisis following oligomycin mediated respiratory restriction during early CD8+ T cell activation.
source: Taken together, these results reveal a matrix-specific energetic crisis following oligomycin mediated respiratory restriction during early CD8+ T cell activation, and suggest that inhibition of TCA cycle and substrate-level phosphorylation may be the central inhibitory mechanism of respiratory restriction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Inhibition of TCA cycle and substrate-level phosphorylation may be the central inhibitory mechanism of respiratory restriction.
source: Taken together, these results reveal a matrix-specific energetic crisis following oligomycin mediated respiratory restriction during early CD8+ T cell activation, and suggest that inhibition of TCA cycle and substrate-level phosphorylation may be the central inhibitory mechanism of respiratory restriction.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: TCA-linked substrate-level phosphorylation is thought to fuel mitochondrial matrix activity, while ATP synthase-derived ATP is exported to the cytoplasm.
source: TCA-linked substrate-level phosphorylation is thought to fuel mitochondrial matrix activity, while ATP synthase-derived ATP is exported to the cytoplasm (Schwimmer et al., 2005; Bochud-Allemann and Schneider, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Treatment of stimulated CD8+ T cells with both oligomycin and FCCP led to an almost complete rescue of CD25 expression compared to the cells treated with only oligomycin.
source: Strikingly, treatment of stimulated CD8+ T cells with both oligomycin and FCCP led to an almost complete rescue of CD25 expression (Figure 5A-B) and proliferation (Figure 5C-D) compared to the cells treated with only oligomycin.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Treatment of stimulated CD8+ T cells with both oligomycin and FCCP led to an almost complete rescue of proliferation compared to the cells treated with only oligomycin.
source: Strikingly, treatment of stimulated CD8+ T cells with both oligomycin and FCCP led to an almost complete rescue of CD25 expression (Figure 5A-B) and proliferation (Figure 5C-D) compared to the cells treated with only oligomycin.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Uncoupling the respiratory chain from ATP synthase rescues the respiratory-restricted T-Early cells.
source: These key observations demonstrate that uncoupling the respiratory chain from ATP synthase rescues the respiratory-restricted T-Early cells, suggesting that the inhibitory mechanism that follows respiratory restriction is linked to a decrease in ATP concentration in the matrix compartment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FCCP rescue data in Figure 5A-D.

claim: The inhibitory mechanism that follows respiratory restriction is linked to a decrease in ATP concentration in the matrix compartment.
source: These key observations demonstrate that uncoupling the respiratory chain from ATP synthase rescues the respiratory-restricted T-Early cells, suggesting that the inhibitory mechanism that follows respiratory restriction is linked to a decrease in ATP concentration in the matrix compartment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FCCP rescue data in Figure 5A-D.

claim: T-Early cells treated with oligomycin and FCCP exhibited significantly higher ATP and lower AMP/GMP concentrations compared to controls treated with only oligomycin.
source: As expected, T-Early cells treated with oligomycin and FCCP exhibited significantly higher ATP and lower AMP/GMP concentrations compared to controls treated with only oligomycin (Figure 5E-F).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data in Figure 5E-F.

claim: The increase of cellular ATP and reductions of AMP and GMP may be primarily attributed to matrix-bound substrate-level phosphorylation.
source: Given the ATP synthase blockade, the increase of cellular ATP and reductions of AMP and GMP may be primarily attributed to matrix-bound substrate-level phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolomics data in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Respiratory restriction yielded marked increases of several key TCA cycle metabolites—including succinate, malate, and citrate—compared to control.
source: In line with our hypothesis, respiratory restriction yielded marked increases of several key TCA cycle metabolites—including succinate, malate, and citrate—compared to control (Figure 5G and its source data).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glutamine tracing data in Figure 5G.

claim: Relative to controls, oligomycin treatment led to increased levels of glutamate and aspartate.
source: Additionally, relative to controls, oligomycin treatment led to increased levels of glutamate and aspartate, which are linked to the TCA cycle via the Gaba Shunt and the malate-aspartate shuttle, respectively (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glutamine tracing data in Figure 5G.

claim: The addition of FCCP to oligomycin-treated T-Early cells reduced the signal levels of all TCA-linked intermediates, indicating stimulation of the TCA cycle.
source: Importantly, the addition of FCCP to oligomycin-treated T-Early cells reduced the signal levels of all TCA-linked intermediates, indicating stimulation of the TCA cycle (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glutamine tracing data in Figure 5G.

claim: During early activation, OXPHOS is required primarily to provide ATP for mitochondrial-biogenesis.
source: Our findings demonstrated that during early activation, OXPHOS is required primarily to provide ATP for mitochondrial-biogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The build-up of additional mitochondrial biomass is a critical checkpoint in T cell activation.
source: It is thought that the build-up of additional mitochondrial biomass is a critical checkpoint in T cell activation (Ron-Harel et al., 2016; Buck et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Following the mitochondrial-biogenesis checkpoint, fully activated CD8+ T cells show only a marginal reduction in proliferation capacity under hypoxic conditions.
source: Following the mitochondrial-biogenesis checkpoint, fully activated CD8+ T cells show only a marginal reduction in proliferation capacity under hypoxic conditions (Doedens et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: During systemic hypoxia, activated CD8+ T cells are arrested at the mitochondrial-biogenesis checkpoint.
source: Thus, our results suggest that during systemic hypoxia, activated CD8+ T cells are arrested at the mitochondrial-biogenesis checkpoint, and might thus be rescued by short oxygen resuscitation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Activated CD8+ T cells arrested at the mitochondrial-biogenesis checkpoint might be rescued by short oxygen resuscitation.
source: Thus, our results suggest that during systemic hypoxia, activated CD8+ T cells are arrested at the mitochondrial-biogenesis checkpoint, and might thus be rescued by short oxygen resuscitation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: CD8+ T cells that were activated under hypoxia and then re-exposed to atmospheric oxygen pressure exhibited significantly increased CD25 expression and proliferative capacity.
source: In contrast, CD8+ T cells that were activated under hypoxia and then re-exposed to atmospheric oxygen pressure exhibited significantly increased CD25 expression and proliferative capacity (Figure 6B-E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6B-E.

claim: Compared to mice kept under systemic hypoxia for 72 hr, the hypoxic mice that were resuscitated at atmospheric oxygen for 48 hr exhibited a significantly improved anti-lentiviral CD8+ T cell response.
source: In line with the in vitro results, compared to mice kept under systemic hypoxia for 72 hr, the hypoxic mice that were resuscitated at atmospheric oxygen for 48 hr exhibited a significantly improved anti-lentiviral CD8+ T cell response, manifested by a marked increase in proliferative capacity (Figure 6G–H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6G-H.

claim: Resuscitation at atmospheric oxygen pressure led to increased mtDendra2 expression compared to mice kept under hypoxia for 72 hr.
source: Importantly, resuscitation at atmospheric oxygen pressure also led to increased mtDendra2 expression compared to mice kept under hypoxia for 72 hr (Figure 6I–J).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6I-J.

claim: The CD8+ response was strongly inhibited under continuous systemic hypoxia.
source: As expected, our analysis of CD62L, CD44, and CD25 revealed that the CD8+ response was strongly inhibited under continuous systemic hypoxia.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6L-Q.

claim: In the transient resuscitation group, a marked increase in the population of OVA-associated CD44+, CD25+, CD62L− CD8+ T cells was observed.
source: In contrast, in the transient resuscitation group, we observed a marked increase in the population of OVA-associated CD44+, CD25+, CD62L− CD8+ T cells (Figure 6L–Q and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6L-Q.
